answer:
Represent positions as \(N\) (winning for the next player) or \(P\) (losing for the next player). Since landing on \(13\) wins immediately, treat \(13\) as a terminal \(P\)-position for the player whose turn would be next. A move to \(8\) is forbidden, but a move may jump over it.

\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
n & \text{legal moves} & \text{type}\\ \hline
13 & \varnothing & P \text{ (game already won by previous player)}\\
12 & 13 & N\\
11 & 12 & P\\
10 & 11,13 & N\\
9 & 10,12 & P\\
8 & \text{forbidden landing; unreachable} & -\\
7 & 10 & P \quad (8\text{ forbidden})\\
6 & 7,9 & N\\
5 & 6 & P \quad (8\text{ forbidden})\\
4 & 5,7 & N\\
3 & 4,6 & P\\
2 & 3,5 & N\\
1 & 2,4 & P\\
0 & 1,3 & N
\end{array}
\]

Thus the losing positions for the player to move are

\[
1,3,5,7,9,11,13,
\]

and the winning positions are the even positions together with \(0\), except that \(8\) is an illegal landing place.

From \(0\), the legal first moves are to \(1\) or to \(3\). Both land in \(P\)-positions, so both are winning first moves.

\[
\boxed{\text{The winning first moves from }0\text{ are to stone }1\text{ and to stone }3.}
\]

Verification: from every odd \(P\)-position, any legal move lands on an even \(N\)-position; from every reachable even \(N\)-position, there is a move to an odd \(P\)-position. Therefore the first player wins by moving first to either \(1\) or \(3\), then always returning the marker to one of the listed \(P\)-positions until landing on \(13\).
